meta.reportLabel: Thu - THE OIL SPIKE HAS HALF UNWOUND AND US CPI CAME IN COOL, SO THE BOARD SORTS ON POLICY AGAIN. July CPI printed 3.4% headline from 3.5% and core 2.5% from 2.6%, exactly at consensus, and September hike odds settled near 40% from 44% - the upside tail the crude surge had put on the print never showed up. Crude then reversed: WTI is 82.11 from 83.20 and Brent 88.77, after EIA reported a 17.4 million barrel inventory build, the largest since early 2023, and Vance said Iran has told Washington it has no plans to toll the Strait. That thins CAD's second leg, so CAD is downgraded to +1. The day's biggest single repricing is New Zealand: RBNZ two-year inflation expectations COLLAPSED to 2.34% from 2.53%, the lowest since Q4 2025, and one-year to 2.60% from 3.41% - the one risk to the NZD short resolved the wrong way for kiwi bulls, and NZD goes to -2. UK Q2 GDP was +0.4% q/q with y/y accelerating to 1.2% from 0.9% and June monthly +0.3% against an expected fall, so GBP is upgraded to STRENGTHENING. The yen made new lows past 159 with the 159.36-159.40 band capping a third attempt just under intervention territory. Silver is the standout at 66.20 after a 2.5% session, gold 4,377 off the 4,427 spike. Cleanest trades: EUR/NZD LONG, AUD/NZD LONG, GBP/NZD LONG, EUR/CHF LONG, AUD/JPY LONG, XAG/USD LONG. US PPI at 12:30Z is the only scheduled risk today.

meta.regime: Two sessions ago the regime was geopolitics; today it is policy differentials again, and the rotation was driven by the two things that were supposed to reinforce each other failing to. US July CPI landed exactly on consensus at 3.4% headline and 2.5% core, both a tenth below June, which means the 5% crude surge that ran through Monday and Tuesday did NOT show up in the price data, and the inflation tail the hawks were relying on has been deferred rather than realised - September hike odds settled around 40% from 44% before the release, and bond traders are holding what is effectively a coin-toss. Crude itself then went the other way: WTI is 82.11 against 83.20, Brent 88.77 against 88.91, after the EIA reported a 17.4 million barrel US crude build, the largest weekly increase since early 2023, and after Vice President Vance said Iran has told Washington it has no plans to impose tolls on the Strait of Hormuz - which sits directly against Trump's compensation demand and Iran's own five conditions. The strait is not open and the positions are still far apart, but the market has taken roughly half the risk premium back out, and that is enough to thin the terms-of-trade trade that drove Tuesday. So the sort is back to who is actually moving rates. The euro keeps the cleanest hawkish story into September 10, Australia keeps the highest policy rate in the G10 with an August Statement on Monetary Policy that says inflation does not reach the midpoint until 2028 and risks skew UP, and New Zealand just lost its last argument. Risk appetite is firm underneath all of it - the DAX is around 26,324 near records and the STOXX 600 has been printing record closes - which caps the franc and the yen at the same time.

dailyRead: The single most important thing that happened is a non-event: US July CPI came in at 3.4% headline and 2.5% core, precisely at consensus and a tenth below June on both, with shelter accounting for about two thirds of the 0.1% monthly rise. That matters more than a surprise would have, because the entire hawkish case rebuilt on Monday and Tuesday rested on the argument that a 5% crude surge is an inflation input - and the July data says it has not arrived yet. September hike odds settled around 40% from 44% pre-release, having briefly touched 48% intraday, and Chair Warsh's position remains that he is open to September if inflation rises, which it did not. The dollar is therefore still the weak side of most G10 pairs, but it is basing rather than breaking - the index found support at 99.40 and the residual hawkish reads (initial claims near cycle lows, unit labour costs 1.3%, Cook saying she is prepared to raise) have not gone anywhere. Then crude reversed. WTI is 82.11 from 83.20 and Brent 88.77, undone by an EIA crude build of 17.4 million barrels, the largest since early 2023, and by Vance saying Iran has told Washington it has no plans to toll the Strait, which contradicts the escalatory framing of Trump's compensation demand. The positions have NOT converged - Iran still demands the naval blockade lifted, sanctions lifted, US forces withdrawn, reparations paid and assets released, and it is negotiating only through Oman - but the market has taken back roughly half of Monday's premium, and that is enough to change the FX sort. Canada loses the second of its two legs: the +75,100 July jobs print and 6.4% unemployment are untouched and still the best labour story in the G10, but the terms-of-trade leg has thinned, so CAD comes back from +2 to +1 and NZD/CAD and CAD/JPY go from HIGH to MEDIUM. The day's cleanest currency repricing is New Zealand. The RBNZ quarterly survey showed two-year inflation expectations falling to 2.34% from 2.53%, the lowest since Q4 2025, and one-year expectations collapsing to 2.60% from 3.41% - the largest single-quarter fall in the series in years. Yesterday's note flagged that a JUMP in expectations was the only near-term risk to the NZD short structure; the number went the other way instead, which means the imported-inflation channel from the 27.5% petrol contribution to Q2 CPI is not feeding through to expectations, and the RBNZ has nothing left to answer a 5.6% unemployment rate with. NZD moves to -2 and the kiwi shorts are the highest-conviction book on the sheet. The UK resolved firm on both halves of its data week: Tuesday's labour report held unemployment at 4.9% with wages 4.3% including bonuses and 3.4% excluding, and this morning Q2 GDP printed +0.4% q/q in line, with y/y ACCELERATING to 1.2% from 0.9% and June monthly GDP at +0.3% against an expected small decline. That is not a set of numbers that folds the three BoE dissenters, so GBP is upgraded from MIXED to STRENGTHENING at +1. The euro is unchanged at +2 and remains the cleanest hawkish story - Sept 10 is still around 70% priced, the July HICP at 2.9% with core UP to 2.5% stands on its own, and Lagarde's second-round-effects framing survives an oil pullback that leaves Brent near 89. Australia stays +2 on a two-sided day: Bullock's Tuesday hawkish hold and an August Statement on Monetary Policy that puts underlying inflation at 3.3% by end-2026, does not see the midpoint until 2028 and calls the risks skewed to the UPSIDE, against Assistant Governor Kent this morning saying policy is only somewhat restrictive, that tightening is working as intended, and citing the currency's own appreciation as part of the restraint. Kent stopped short of saying policy is sufficiently restrictive, so the optionality survives. The yen is the weakest currency and goes to -2: USD/JPY pushed past 159 to make new lows on a session where the dollar had cool inflation data, the 159.36-159.40 band has now capped three advances since Aug 10, and Japanese 10-year yields are at a one-month high. That is a currency failing on its own account, not on dollar strength - but with the 160 handle a few pips away and a record joint MoF/US Treasury operation only two weeks old, this is a currency to be short through the crosses and NOT through USD/JPY. The franc holds at -1: the haven bid is fading with gold back to 4,377 from the 4,427 CPI spike and European equities near records, the SNB is at zero until at least Sept 24, and CHF crosses against EUR and AUD are the cleanest expression. Silver is the standout in the commodity complex, up 2.5% to 66.20 and outperforming gold decisively, because it is getting the soft-CPI real-rates leg AND an industrial leg from firm global risk appetite and the AI-investment demand the RBA itself flagged. Gold stays constructive but has given back the spike. USOIL goes to RANGE - the inventory build and the deal chatter on one side, an unresolved strait on the other, and no edge in the middle. US PPI at 12:30Z is the only scheduled event today; with final demand running 5.5% y/y in June and the crude move now partly unwound, it is the pipeline check on whether August CPI gets the energy pass-through July avoided.

USD.note: Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 for a fifth straight meeting with THREE dissents FOR a hike, and Chair Warsh declined to give guidance or submit a dot. The two inputs since have pulled in opposite directions and netted to a coin-toss. First, Aug 7 payrolls: July nonfarm payrolls CONTRACTED by 23,000 against +83,000 to +95,000 expected, the prior two months were revised down by a combined 146,000, June was cut to +20,000, and the fall in unemployment to 4.1% from 4.2% is a participation artefact with participation at a five-year low of 61.4%. Average hourly earnings slowed to 3.2% y/y, the weakest since May 2021. Second, and decisively, July CPI on Aug 12 came in EXACTLY at consensus - 3.4% headline against 3.5% in June, core 2.5% against 2.6%, and just +0.1% m/m with shelter about two thirds of that. The significance is what did not happen: the 5% crude surge of Aug 10-11 produced no visible pass-through, so the inflation tail the hawks were pricing has been deferred. September hike odds settled around 40% from 44% before the release after briefly touching 48%. The residual hawkish reads remain real and unchanged - Warsh has said he is open to September if inflation rises, Lisa Cook said in Anchorage she is prepared to raise rates, initial claims are at a cycle-low four-week average of 198,750, announced layoffs are the lowest in two years and unit labour costs rose just 1.3%. Q2 GDP 1.5%. July PPI today at 12:30Z is the pipeline check - final demand was running 5.5% y/y in June - and then Jackson Hole on Aug 27 is where Warsh has to frame September.

EUR.when: Sept 10 (~70% priced, still the cleanest hawkish story)
EUR.note: Deposit facility 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike, headline refi 2.40% and marginal lending 2.65%, all confirmed unchanged on Jul 23 and verified on TE today. TE's own end-of-quarter model carries 2.65% on the refi, i.e. one more 25bp move by end-September. The July communication is still the operative text: the ECB warned the full inflationary impact of the energy shock has yet to emerge, and Lagarde said the longer energy prices remain elevated the more likely they are to drive broader inflation through indirect and second-round effects. Today's crude pullback to Brent 88.77 does NOT break that - the level that matters is the level, and Brent near 89 against the June projections is still an energy channel that is open, with euro-area energy inflation having accelerated to 10.0% from 8.5% in July. The domestic leg stands entirely on its own and is the reason EUR is the top score: July HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5%, services inflation 3.3%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, final composite PMI 52.0 with services 51.7 and manufacturing 51.9 (an 8-month high in business activity), wage growth 3.4%, unemployment 6.3% and stable, ZEW economic sentiment 23.4 from 9.5. The honest counterargument is pipeline disinflation - producer prices decelerating to 4.6% y/y from 5.9%, food inflation at 1.2%, June retail sales falling 0.3% m/m - and the ECB's own post-July 'wait-and-see' tone. But nothing between Jul 23 and today has removed the September hike from the curve.

GBP.when: Sept 17 (Jul 30 = 6-3 hold; the dissenters have not folded)
GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus. Sterling's two-week data vacuum has now been filled and it resolved firm on both halves. Tuesday's labour report: unemployment 4.9% with 1.76 million unemployed, wages 4.3% including bonuses and 3.4% excluding, real pay positive at 1.3% and 0.4% respectively, employment rate 75.1%. This morning's Q2 GDP: +0.4% q/q in line with consensus, a slowdown from Q1's +0.6%, but with the y/y rate ACCELERATING to 1.2% from 0.9% and - the standout - June monthly GDP at +0.3% against expectations of a slight decline, with real GDP per head up 0.4% on the quarter and 1.0% on the year. An economy that grew through the early months of the Iran war and is accelerating on a y/y basis does not fold three dissenters on a committee that is already the most inflation-sensitive in the G10. June CPI was 2.6% with core 2.6% and services 3.6%. The genuine soft spots are the labour market's edges: vacancies fell to 712,000, below pre-pandemic levels, economic inactivity is rising with 9.11 million inactive at a 20.9% rate, and the claimant count rose 6.7k. TE's end-of-quarter forecast is 4.00%. July CPI around Aug 19 is the next real input.

JPY.when: Sept 18 (October still the live window; intervention is the nearer risk)
JPY.note: Held 1.00% on Jul 31 8-1, Takata dissenting for 1.25%. The domestic case is the best in three decades and is not the problem: June labour cash earnings +3.4% y/y with base pay accelerating to 3.4% from 3.0%, real earnings positive for a sixth month, nominal growth above 3% for five straight months - the longest run in 34 years. The Bank has warned for the first time that underlying inflation could exceed target and said discussions will focus on upside price risks. June CPI rose to 1.7% from 1.5% with core at 1.6%, and Tokyo July core CPI jumped to 1.9% from 1.6%. Japanese 10-year yields are at a one-month high, which normally supports a currency. The problem is that none of it is transmitting. The yen weakened past 159 per dollar on the SAME session that US CPI came in cool - a currency losing ground when its counterpart gets dovish data is failing on its own account, and it has now retraced about half the gains from the record joint MoF/US Treasury operation at the end of July that spiked USD/JPY to 155.20 from 40-year lows. The 159.36-159.40 band has capped three advances since Aug 10, just under the round 160.00. Today's crude pullback helps the JPY 407bn trade deficit at the margin but has not turned it. This is why JPY is downgraded to -2. Q2 GDP lands Aug 16 23:50Z and July national CPI around Aug 20 23:30Z. Above 160 the risk is not technical - it is a second official operation that reverses every yen cross in minutes, which is exactly why yen shorts belong in EUR/JPY, AUD/JPY and GBP/JPY rather than USD/JPY.

AUD.when: Sept 29 (Aug 11 = hawkish hold at 4.35%; the cycle is not declared over)
AUD.note: Held the cash rate at 4.35% on Aug 11 as all 37 Reuters economists and all four majors expected, but the tone did the work: Bullock said the domestic economy is operating ABOVE CAPACITY and that growth will need to slow to bring inflation down, and the statement retained the line 'including increasing the cash rate target further if required' with no qualification. The August Statement on Monetary Policy published alongside it is the hawkish anchor - underlying inflation is forecast at 3.3% by end-2026, inflation is NOT expected to return to the middle of the 2-3% band until early 2028, and the risks to inflation are explicitly judged to be skewed to the UPSIDE, citing elevated energy prices and strong AI-related demand. That is the highest policy rate in the G10 after three hikes in 2026 (Feb 3.85%, Mar 4.10%, May 4.35%). Against that, Assistant Governor Kent this morning said policy is only 'somewhat restrictive', that earlier tightening is working as intended and demand moderation is 'intended and needed', and he named the Australian dollar's own year-to-date appreciation as part of the restraint - a mild dovish shading, though he pointedly stopped short of saying policy is sufficiently restrictive, so the optionality survives. Q2 detail supports the hawks: headline CPI cooled to 3.8% from 4.0% and trimmed mean held 3.6%, but the WEIGHTED MEDIAN ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0%. Labour is solid - employment +76,343 in June, unemployment 4.4%, participation 67.0%. July PMIs strong at services 53.6, composite 53.2, manufacturing 52.0; consumer confidence 83.9; June trade a AUD 1,929m surplus; commodity prices +15.4% y/y. TE's model carries 4.60%. The dovish input remains July consumer inflation expectations at 4.7% from 5.5%.

NZD.when: Sept 2 (the hike is off, and today's survey confirmed it)
NZD.note: OCR raised 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years, and that cycle is now finished with the evidence to prove it. Today's RBNZ quarterly survey of expectations is the confirmation: two-year inflation expectations FELL to 2.34% from 2.53%, the lowest reading since Q4 2025, and one-year expectations collapsed to 2.60% from 3.41% - one of the largest single-quarter falls in the series. Only the five- and ten-year tails ticked up, to 2.31% and 2.20%. Yesterday the risk flagged against the NZD short was a JUMP in expectations forcing a rethink; it went decisively the other way, which means the imported-inflation channel that drove Q2 CPI to 4.1% - 27.5% of which was petrol - is not feeding through to what businesses actually expect, and today's crude pullback to WTI 82 removes some of the fuel for it too. Note the survey's own OCR question still shows respondents expecting 2.73% by end-September and 3.21% in a year, but that section was conducted on stale footing (the survey was run relative to the May decision) and is contradicted by the expectations data itself. Meanwhile the labour side is the worst in the G10: Q2 unemployment 5.6% against 5.4% expected, the highest since Q3 2015; underutilisation 13.8%; labour cost index slowed to 2.1% y/y; employment +0.5% q/q only because participation climbed to 70.7% from 70.4%. Core inflation 3.2%. The only offset remains domestic sentiment - July ANZ business confidence 56.1 from 36.6, ANZ Roy Morgan consumer confidence 99.3, manufacturing PMI 59.7, composite 53.6 - but ANZ commodity prices decelerated to +0.5% y/y from +2.7%, which takes the terms-of-trade support away too.

CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting, verified on TE today, and nothing since changes that because the inflation side is still undershooting - June CPI 2.8% with CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9%, both BELOW target, and core at 2.1%. The labour leg is intact and is the best in the G10: July employment rose 75,100, the largest gain in two years, with full-time +38,600 and part-time +36,600, unemployment falling to a two-year low of 6.4% from 6.5% and participation rising to 65.1%; core-aged women's unemployment fell 0.3pp to 5.2% and youth unemployment dropped to 12.6% from an April peak of 14.3%. Average hourly wages rose a soft 2.8% y/y to $37.17, which is why this is a growth story and not a rate one. What has changed today is the second leg. Tuesday's terms-of-trade upgrade rested on WTI breaking out of 78.82 into the low 80s; crude has now given back part of it, with WTI at 82.11 down 1.39% and Brent 88.77, after the EIA reported a 17.4 million barrel US crude build - the largest weekly increase since early 2023 - and after Vance said Iran has no plans to toll the Strait. WTI at 82 is still comfortably above last week's 78.82, so the leg is thinner rather than gone, but it is no longer strong enough to justify a +2 alongside the euro and the Australian dollar. CAD comes back to +1 on labour, and the CAD-versus-oil trades (NZD/CAD, CAD/JPY, USOIL) all step down a conviction notch. Q1 GDP was flat at 0.0% q/q with monthly GDP +0.2% in June. July CPI is due around Aug 18.

CHF.note: At ZERO since mid-2025, held in Dec, Mar and Jun, verified on TE today; panellists see no change until 2027. July CPI came in at 0.4% y/y against 0.5% expected, down from 0.5%, with core unchanged at 0.3% - under the SNB's own 0.7% Q3 conditional forecast. July unemployment rose to 3.0% from 2.9% with unemployed persons at 139,276, adding a growth argument to the inflation undershoot, and producer and import prices are deflating at -2.1% y/y. The June statement pledged to lean against rapid APPRECIATION only, so the SNB is content to let the franc slide. The case for pressing franc shorts is better today than it was on Tuesday: the haven complex has cooled with gold back to 4,377 from the 4,427 post-CPI spike, crude has given back half its surge, and European equities are near records with the DAX around 26,324 and the STOXX 600 printing record closes. The standing cautions have not disappeared - FX reserves rose to CHF 768.3bn in July from 758.9bn, and the Hormuz impasse is genuinely unresolved with Iran negotiating only through Oman - so the discipline stands: trade the franc through crosses with a real rate or growth story (EUR/CHF, AUD/CHF) rather than through USD/CHF, where a weak dollar and a weak franc simply cancel. Domestic activity is also turning up hard - services PMI 63.9 from 59.8, business confidence 104, ZEW economic sentiment +10 from -25.

strength.forward: 🔻 The cleanest short on the board. The single risk flagged against this structure - a jump in inflation expectations - resolved decisively the other way, which says the 27.5% petrol contribution to Q2's 4.1% CPI is not reaching expectations, and today's crude pullback removes more of the fuel. Hold on Sept 2 and the cycle is over at 2.50%. strength.forward: ⚖️ Downgraded to -2. The domestic case is the strongest in three decades and 10-year yields are at a one-month high, yet the currency lost ground on a dovish-dollar day - that is idiosyncratic weakness, not dollar strength, and it persists until the October window. catalysts.note: The only scheduled risk today and the pipeline check on the crude surge. Final demand was running 5.5% y/y in June with the monthly index falling 0.3%. July CPI showed no energy pass-through - if PPI shows it building at the producer level, the September hike case rebuilds for August CPI and the dollar base at 99.40 holds.

The consumer check after a contracting payroll print and a cool CPI. Wage growth at 3.2% is now below headline inflation at 3.4%, which squeezes real purchasing power - a weak number compounds the labour story and extends the dollar short.

Watch the inflation-expectations components rather than the headline, given how much weight the market is putting on whether the energy shock is reaching expectations - the same question New Zealand just answered in the negative.

Q1 was +0.5% q/q and +0.6% y/y. Arrives with the yen already at -2 and USD/JPY pressing 159 - a weak print tightens the intervention question rather than the policy one, since the BoJ's October window is set by wages, not growth.

June was 2.8% with CPI-trim 1.8% and CPI-median 1.9%, both below target - the reason the BoC stays on hold Sept 2 despite the best labour market in the G10. A move back above 2% in the core measures would give CAD the rate leg it currently lacks.

June was 2.6% headline and core with services at 3.6%. This is the input that decides whether sterling's upgrade holds - a firm services print keeps the three BoE dissenters alive into Sept 17 and validates GBP/NZD and GBP/JPY; a soft one folds them and takes the hawkish tail out.

June was 1.7% with core 1.6%, and Tokyo's July core already jumped to 1.9% from 1.6%, which points to an upside national print. The BoJ has warned underlying inflation could exceed target - a strong number builds the October case even if the currency cannot express it yet.

Chair Warsh's first Jackson Hole. He declined to give guidance or submit a dot in July and has since said he is open to a September hike if inflation rises - it did not in July, so this is where he has to say whether the deferred energy tail still counts.

catalysts.event: Iran/US impasse and Strait of Hormuz status
catalysts.note: Positions hardened this week then blurred. Trump demands compensation for deaths and injuries and says the US controls the strait; Iran demands the naval blockade lifted, sanctions lifted, US forces withdrawn, reparations paid and frozen assets released, and is negotiating only with Oman, proposing shared management. Against that, Vance said he is confident of a deal and that Iran has told Washington it has no plans to impose tolls. The June 14-point MoU unravelled in days, so treat deal headlines as reversible. Crude has taken back about half of Monday's 5% premium.

catalysts.event: MoF / US Treasury yen intervention watch
catalysts.note: USD/JPY past 159 with the 159.36-159.40 band capping three advances since Aug 10. The record joint operation at end-July spiked it to 155.20 from 40-year lows and was not followed up. Above 160 the risk is a second official operation that reverses every yen cross in minutes - which is why the yen shorts belong in EUR/JPY, AUD/JPY and GBP/JPY.

Around 70% priced for a 25bp move on the deposit facility to 2.50%, with TE's model carrying 2.65% on the refi by end-quarter. This is the single largest scheduled catalyst on the sheet - it is the engine under EUR/NZD, EUR/CHF, EUR/JPY and EUR/USD, and a hold would unwind the euro's +2 in one session.
Roughly a coin-toss at around 40% for a hike to 4.00% on the upper bound, with three dissents FOR a hike already on record in July. Every dollar position on the sheet resolves here.

geopolitics: The war is unresolved and the strait is still not open, but the market spent today taking risk premium out rather than putting it in, and the FX consequences follow that. The escalatory track is intact on paper: Trump said this week that the US controls the Strait of Hormuz and demanded Iran compensate victims' families and regional states for deaths and injuries linked to decades of conflict, while Iran's Supreme National Security Council answered with its full list of conditions for reopening - lift the naval blockade, lift sanctions, withdraw US forces from the region, pay war reparations and release frozen Iranian assets - and Tehran has said it could prolong the war. Iran is refusing to negotiate directly with Washington and is talking only to Oman, proposing shared future management of the waterway. Against that, three things pushed the other way in the last 24 hours. Vice President Vance said he is confident of a deal and, critically, that Iran has told the US it has no plans to impose tolls on the strait - the toll question being the commercial core of the dispute. The EIA reported US crude inventories rose 17.4 million barrels last week, the largest weekly build since early 2023, which says the physical market is not tight even with transit traffic subdued. And the price followed: WTI is 82.11, down 1.39% from Tuesday's 83.20 close, and Brent 88.77 from 88.91, giving back roughly half of the 5% surge that drove Monday and Tuesday's whole FX sort. The transmission into currencies is therefore a partial reversal rather than a regime change. Canada loses the thinner half of its bid and comes back to +1, with NZD/CAD and CAD/JPY stepping down from HIGH to MEDIUM conviction and USOIL moving to RANGE. Japan gets marginal relief on the JPY 407bn trade deficit but not enough to change a currency that made new lows past 159 anyway. New Zealand's imported-petrol channel loses fuel at exactly the moment its inflation expectations collapsed to 2.34%, which is why the kiwi short is now the cleanest structure on the sheet. The euro is the least affected, because Lagarde's second-round-effects case rests on Brent near 89 rather than on Brent at 92. The franc and the yen are both capped by firm risk appetite - the DAX around 26,324 near records and the STOXX 600 printing record closes on cheaper crude - and gold has come back to 4,377 from the 4,427 spike, confirming the haven bid is draining. The asymmetry to respect: the June 14-point MoU mediated by Pakistan and Qatar unravelled within days of signing, so any deal headline is reversible, and a fresh strike or tanker incident puts the entire premium back faster than it came out.
